intro: After the Second Symphony’s funeral march comes a dance for strings in A♭ major. Each return brings a small surprise: a new cello melody, then the whole tune plucked with the fingertips.

sections.label: A · A♭ major: the strings dance
B · Running triplets in the strings
sections.mNote: A horn introduces the minor-key episode

sections.label: A′ · The cellos add a tune
sections.mNote: A flowing cello melody beneath the familiar dance

cues.title: A dance for strings
cues.text: The strings begin a Ländler, an Austrian country dance in three. A♭ major sounds wonderfully comfortable after the first movement’s C minor. Mahler writes Sehr gemächlich — very leisurely — and adds another warning: Nie eilen, never hurry.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement II, p. 57: A♭ major, 3/8, opening string parts and tempo directions.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Triplets under the horn
cues.text: A horn ushers in running triplets. At first only a few string players take them up; the little figures spread through the desks. The tune has turned to the minor, but Mahler still asks for a leisurely pace.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, p. 58, rehearsal 3: horn figure, reduced string desks, triplets and Nicht eilen. Sehr gemächlich. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: July at the lake
cues.text: At Steinbach am Attersee in July 1893, Mahler works on three very different movements: this dance, the fish-sermon scherzo and Urlicht. He dates the Andante’s orchestral draft 30 July, eleven days after the song.
cues.evidence: Manuscript dates for the scherzo, Urlicht and Andante: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Two tunes at once
cues.text: The Ländler returns to A♭ major. Above, the violins have their old dance; beneath, the cellos sing a new, flowing melody. The cellos keep their bows on the strings while the double basses pluck the beat.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 61–62, rehearsal 5: return to Tempo I, added cello line and pizzicato double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two pianos first
cues.text: With the support of two wealthy Hamburg industrialists, Hofmeister of Leipzig publishes the symphony first in Hermann Behn’s two-piano arrangement, in 1896, then as a full score, in February 1897.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score (December 2010); the February 1897 date: Mahler Foundation, https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/. https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: The triplets grow teeth
cues.text: The minor-key episode returns with winds and brass joining the strings. Those once-delicate triplets now drive a full orchestral passage. The country dance has a storm in its middle.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, second contrasting episode, pp. 64–72. The movement’s alternating dance and triplet sections are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Episodes from the hero’s life
cues.text: In a letter of 1896 Mahler calls the Andante and the Scherzo “episodes from the life of the fallen hero”. The first movement, he writes there, is the hero’s titanic struggle with life and fate, and his death.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s letter of 1896 on the symphony, quoted by the Mahler Foundation: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-manuscript/

cues.title: Berlin hears three movements
cues.text: On 4 March 1895, Mahler conducts the first three movements in Berlin. The Andante and scherzo follow the funeral march, and the concert stops there. Urlicht and the choral finale reach the public that December.
cues.evidence: Partial première on 4 March and complete première on 13 December 1895: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: The dance on fingertips
cues.text: The strings pluck the returning Ländler. Its familiar tune becomes a collection of small, dry notes, with flute, piccolo and harp adding bright touches above. A♭ major is home again.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 73–74, rehearsal 12: Tempo I, pizzicato strings, piccolo, flute and harp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The summer composer arrives
cues.text: By about 20 June 1893 Mahler and his household, Natalie Bauer-Lechner among them, have retreated to Steinbach am Attersee. He turns first to this Andante, and completes its sketch, though not yet its orchestration, in about seven days.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score of Symphony No. 2 (December 2010). https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

transitions.title: A horn starts the triplets
transitions.from: A · A♭ major: the strings dance
transitions.to: B · Running triplets in the strings
transitions.how: The A♭-major dance turns to the minor. A soft horn figure starts the triplets; only a few string desks join at first. Flute, clarinet and harp enter as the passage grows. The score repeats Nicht eilen: the quicker notes keep the leisurely beat.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister full score (1897), movement II, p. 58, rehearsal 3; reduced string desks and Nicht eilen. Sehr gemächlich.

transitions.title: A cello melody joins the dance
transitions.from: B · Running triplets in the strings
transitions.to: A′ · The cellos add a tune
transitions.how: The triplets slow and subside. At rehearsal 5 the score asks for the opening tempo, and the A♭-major Ländler returns. The cellos add a sustained countermelody below the violins while the double basses keep plucking.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 61–62: rehearsal 5, In Tempo I zurückkehren, cello countermelody and pizzicato basses.

transitions.title: Winds and brass take up the triplets
transitions.from: A′ · The cellos add a tune
transitions.how: The second triplet episode brings winds and brass into the running string figures. The short notes that began with a few players now occupy the orchestra, with longer wind phrases stretching above them.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 64–72, the expanded second triplet episode.

transitions.title: The strings put down their bows
transitions.how: The running figures dwindle to short fragments. At rehearsal 12 Mahler restores the opening tempo and A♭ major, but marks the strings pizzicato. Flute, piccolo and harp decorate the plucked melody as it passes through the string sections.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 73–74, rehearsal 12 and the following Tempo I.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Second movement, pp. 57–79: string Ländler, triplet episodes, added cello melody and the plucked return at rehearsal 12.

timeline.note: The strings begin the Ländler, with divided inner parts and a measured bass.
A horn starts the triplets with a few string desks; flute, clarinet and harp join them.
The dance returns with an expressive cello countermelody below the upper strings.
Winds and brass join the strings in the second triplet episode.
Long phrases in flutes and violins stretch above divided strings playing triplets.
The strings pluck the returning dance; piccolo, flute and harp add short decorations.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
